Q: CreateProcess STATUS_DLL_NOT_FOUND - which dll? A:

Unfortunately, there is no API for determining the missing library. Your only option would be to manually access and enumerate the executable's IMPORTS table to find out what DLLs it uses, and then recursively access and enumerate their IMPORTS tables, manually checking every DLL reference you find to see whether that DLL file exists on the OS's search path or not.

Q: I can't remove python pip A:

If you are a Windows user, make sure you run 'python -m pip uninstall pip' in administrator mode.

Q: Should I try to use as many queues as possible? A:

Yes, if you have workload that is highly independent use separate queues.

If the queues need a lot of synchronization between themselves, it may kill any potential benefit you may get.

Basically what you are doing is supplying GPU with some alternative work it can do (and fill stalls and bubbles and idles with and giving GPU the choice) in the case of same queue family. And there is some potential to better use CPU (e.g. singlethreaded vs one queue per thread).

Using separate transfer queues (or other specialized family) seem to be the recommended approach even.

That is generally speaking. More realistic, empirical, sceptical and practical view was already presented by SW and NB answers. In reality one does have to be bit more cautious as those queues target the same resources, have same limits, and other common restrictions, limiting potential benefits gained from this. Notably, if the driver does the wrong thing with multiple queues, it may be very very bad for cache.

This AMD's Leveraging asynchronous queues for concurrent execution(2016) discusses a bit how it maps to their HW\driver. It shows potential benefits of using separate queue families. It says that although they offer two queues of compute family, they did not observe benefits in apps at that time. They say they have only one graphics queue, and why.

NVIDIA seems to have a similar idea of "asynch compute". Shown in Moving to Vulkan: Asynchronous compute.

To be safe, it seems we should still stick with only one graphics, and one async compute queue though on current HW. 16 queues seem like a trap and a way to hurt yourself.

With transfer queues it is not as simple as it seems either. You should use the dedicated ones for Host->Device transfers. And the non-dedicated should be used for device->device transfer ops.

Q: gganimate::animate() warns "font family not found in Windows font database" even when using ragg A:

The only way I could get it to work was to manually install the fonts, and use the suggestion from @M--.

Workflow:

  • close R
  • go to and download the fonts from https://fonts.google.com/specimen/EB+Garamond and https://fonts.google.com/specimen/IBM+Plex+Sans
  • unzip files
  • right-click to manually install the fonts using either "Install for all users" option if you have admin rights or "Install" if not.

Then:

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(showtext)
library(ggtext)
library(gganimate)

# Get system font paths and filter
sys_fonts <- systemfonts::system_fonts()

fp <- sys_fonts[
  grepl("IBM\\s*Plex|EB\\s*Garamond", sys_fonts$family, ignore.case = TRUE), 
  c("name", "path")
]

# Use if "Install for all users" option e.g. admin rights
fp1 <- fp %>% 
  filter(!grepl("AppData", path, ignore.case = TRUE))

# or if no admin rights and installed to AppData
fp1 <- fp %>% 
  filter(grepl("AppData", path, ignore.case = TRUE))

showtext_auto()
showtext_opts(dpi = 300)

# Add fonts
font_add(
  family  = "EB Garamond",
  regular = fp1$path[fp1$name == "EBGaramond-Regular"]
)

font_add(
  family  = "IBM Plex Sans",
  regular = fp1$path[fp1$name == "IBMPlexSans-Regular"]
)

# Register in Windows DB
windowsFonts("IBM Plex Sans" = windowsFont("IBM Plex Sans"))
windowsFonts("EB Garamond" = windowsFont("EB Garamond"))

The rest of your code remains the same. Note that your text colours are white so will not show based on your current plot parameters.

Q: Should (double)(std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) be 2048.0 or 2049.0? A:

It doesn't happen only with float16_t but also any floating-point types narrower than long double. The C standard defines FLT_EVAL_METHOD which was incorporated into C++:

Specifies the precision in which all floating-point arithmetic operations other than assignment and cast are done.

Value Explanation
negative values except -1 implementation-defined behavior
-1 the default precision is not known
0 all operations and constants evaluate in the range and precision of the type used.
Additionally, float_t and double_t are equivalent to float and double respectively
1 all operations and constants evaluate in the range and precision of double.
Additionally, both float_t and double_t are equivalent to double
2 all operations and constants evaluate in the range and precision of long double.
Additionally, both float_t and double_t are equivalent to long double

You can see lots of similar issues where the result doesn't match expectations when FLT_EVAL_METHOD > 1 in C and C++ like:

  • Does any floating point-intensive code produce bit-exact results in any x86-based architecture?
  • Is C floating-point non-deterministic?
  • Difference in floating point arithmetics between x86 and x64
  • different behaviour or sqrt when compiled with 64 or 32 bits
  • std::pow produce different result in 32 bit and 64 bit application
  • acos(double) gives different result on x64 and x32 Visual Studio

You can find more information about this with the keyword "deterministic floating-point math"

The standard wasn't updated to include newer types for FLT_EVAL_METHOD but compilers already made extensions for that. Here's what GCC says about half float:

On x86 targets with SSE2 enabled, without -mavx512fp16, all operations are emulated by software emulation and the float instructions. The default behavior for FLT_EVAL_METHOD is to keep the intermediate result of the operation as 32-bit precision. This may lead to inconsistent behavior between software emulation and AVX512-FP16 instructions. Using -fexcess-precision=16 forces round back after each operation.

Using -mavx512fp16 generates AVX512-FP16 instructions instead of software emulation. The default behavior of FLT_EVAL_METHOD is to round after each operation. The same is true with -fexcess-precision=standard and -mfpmath=sse. If there is no -mfpmath=sse, -fexcess-precision=standard alone does the same thing as before, It is useful for code that does not have _Float16 and runs on the x87 FPU.

6.1.5 Half-Precision Floating Point

I've given some detailed analysis here, but in summary:

  • The compiler can calculate expressions with higher precision. It can spill the intermediate result occasionally when there are no more free registers, but we can't control it unless we force a write to memory

  • The compiler can calculate constexpr expressions internally with different (usually expected) precision, so the below snippet may very well produce different values for r1 and r2:

    std::float16_t sum = std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025);
bool r1 = (std::float16_t(1024) + std::float16_t(1025)) != (std::float16_t(2048));
bool r2 = sum != std::float16_t(2048); // pre-calculated entirely in float16_t precision

Deterministic issues were much more common in the past where 32-bit code uses the 80-bit x87 registers while 64-bit code uses SSE2 instead. Nowadays 16-bit floating-point types will have the same issue, because basically almost no platforms have direct support for them in scalar registers, most of the instructions are vector. So to fix it we can

  • Split the expressions into smaller steps, because the compiler will be forced to round or save to memory after each assignment, or

  • Use the proper excess precision options like in GCC's document,

  • Or even better: never use float16_t scalar and always do SIMD vector operations on them

    All 16-bit floating-point types are originally meant to be used as a storage format only, because their precisions are so low to be meaningful in real scalar expressions. So they can appear in audio samples or image pixel values in files, but when reading into memory they'd be converted to another format like IEEE754 single precision, or int32.

    In case precision is less of a concern then there are vectorized operations on 16-bit floats in most modern architectures. For example VADDPH in x86 AVX-512 and FADD Z0.H, P0/M, Z1.H, Z2.H in ARM SVE can add a lot of float16_t in a single instruction. But even when precision and range are important, it's still much much faster to do a vectorized float32_t operation than a loop on scalar floats

Q: Sqlcmd: Error: Microsoft ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server : Data source name not found and no default driver specified A:

if you're running voltdb on docker try this command to access sqlcmd command line:

"docker exec -it [containerId] sqlcmd"

example: "docker exec -it e526d476e6996585d7802dd301813ddd2f0e1b6ef9d0dcfeb65fc8e95aeedb89 sqlcmd"

Q: LoadRunner SSL Certificate issue A:

Try recording without certificate and see weather you can see the request bodies, if not, then you can think of placing client certificates also make sure you are using the right socket, SSL version and cipers to record the application.
